messages.author: 619391dac2e7b793
messages.subject: external validation
parts:
Hello!
It might be a beginner's question (which I am :) ), but I'm trying to support a bifactor model over other models using correlations with external scores (external validation). Is there any better option to do that using lavaan, other then extracting factor scores and correlating them with the scores? 
Any help would be much appreciated :)

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: external validation
parts:
The better approach is to include the other "external" variables in the model where you are estimating your bifactor.  Then the estimated correlations may be unbiased (if the other variables are themselves unbiased), and you avoid the problems of factor indeterminacy and pseudo factor scores.  You also create a more rigorous test for your bifactor model.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: external validation
parts:
If they are dependent on the factors, then yes, like indicators.  If the theory is more general, then treat them like covariates.  If your factors are F1 and F2 and these external variables are A and B, add the lines;
F1 + F2 ~~ A + B
A ~~ B
to be fully explicit.
     You may also wish to specify fixed.x=F in your sem call, if A and B are random variables rather than researcher-controlled manipulations.
--Ed Rigdon

parts:
I do not know exactly the problem, but there are things that *might* help—and won’t take too much effort to check.  First, “can’t compute standard errors” often mean an identification problem.  Your model runs fine without the OBSBREAKS variable, you have said.  It is hard to imagine why adding a covariate would cause an identification problem.  Still, here are things to try.

1.     Maybe lavaan is confused because the covariate is an observed variable.  It might be happier if you create a factor identical to the observed variable and use that.  So if you add these lines to your model syntax:

OBSBREAKS.F =~ 1*OBSBREAKS

OBSBREAKS ~~ 0*OBSBREAKS

and change the current last line to

general ~~ F.OBSBREAKS

that might clear things up for lavaan.  This does not change the mathematics or the interpretation in any way.

2.  Try starting values.  You need at least 2 large loadings per factor (if the factor is correlated with something else).  The loading for the first indicator of each factor will be fixed to 1 by default, so try setting a starting value for the loading for the second indicator for each factor.  Look at the parameter estimates from the results without the covariate to find plausible starting values for these loadings.  So, for example the first line of your model syntax would change to:

data.model<- ' general =~ aQ2 + start(##)*aQ3 + . . .

where ## is your starting value.

--Ed Rigdon

בתאריך יום שבת, 20 בדצמבר 2014 22:30:35 UTC+2, מאת Edward Rigdon:

     If they are dependent on the factors, then yes, like indicators.  If the theory is more general, then treat them like covariates.  If your factors are F1 and F2 and these external variables are A and B, add the lines;

F1 + F2 ~~ A + B

Thank you Ed!

Does that mean treating them like indicators? 

בתאריך יום שבת, 20 בדצמבר 2014 14:07:02 UTC+2, מאת Edward Rigdon:

     The better approach is to include the other "external" variables in the model where you are estimating your bifactor.  Then the estimated correlations may be unbiased (if the other variables are themselves unbiased), and you avoid the problems of factor indeterminacy and pseudo factor scores.  You also create a more rigorous test for your bifactor model.

--Ed Rigdon
